explain: About 2×1092 \times 10^92×109. A parameter is a number the model multiplies something by. Processing one token uses each parameter once: multiply it by an input, then add the product to a running total. That is two operations per parameter, so about 2×1092 \times 10^92×109 per token for a billion parameters. You will build this count properly in the derivation.

prompt: In 32-bit integer arithmetic, what is 2,147,483,647+12{,}147{,}483{,}647 + 12,147,483,647+1?
explain: −2,147,483,648-2{,}147{,}483{,}648−2,147,483,648. The 32 bits wrap around like an odometer, and the top bit of a signed integer means "negative", so one past the largest positive number is the most negative one. Counting the FLOPs of a large model in 32-bit integers overflows silently: 6ND6ND6ND for a 7-billion-parameter model on 2 trillion tokens is about 8×10228 \times 10^{22}8×1022, far past 2×1092 \times 10^92×109.

prompt: How many FLOPs does a dense model with N parameters spend per token, forward only and in training?
answer: Each parameter takes part in one multiply-add per token, which is 2 FLOPs, so a forward pass costs about 2N FLOPs per token. Training adds a backward pass that computes two products per weight (the gradient for the input and for the weight), about 4N more, so about 6N FLOPs per token.
